_capture.provenance: SYNTHETIC — and unlike the /me/* GET fixtures this one could not be a recording even in principle: these are REQUEST bodies, and obtaining a real one means writing a thread and a message to a live staging account, which the slot 16-47 capture explicitly refused ('This capture performed ZERO writes to the account', manifest-authenticated.md). B2-AC-36's 'real recorded staging payloads' standard is therefore reported NOT EVALUATED with that reason and never PASS (specs.md § 2.2 Finding I, B9-AC-57). expected_body is DERIVED, not recorded: each one is what CustomerServiceChat.tsx:106/:109/:112 over client.ts:243's JSON.stringify produces for that input, computed by applying the source's own transform (body.trim() then .slice(0,80)) rather than transcribed by eye.
_capture.credential: none — no host was contacted to build this file
_capture.why_lao: The one real transform in B9 is subject = trim().slice(0,80), and slice operates on UTF-16 CODE UNITS. For ASCII, code units, code points and graphemes coincide, so an ASCII-only fixture passes for every plausible implementation — including the grapheme-based characters.take(80) a careful Dart developer reaches for first. The lao_over_80 case is chosen so the two provably differ (80 code units vs 99), and tier0_chat_payload_test.dart asserts the INEQUALITY as well as the equality: a fixture that stopped discriminating would fail the test rather than pass it. FACTORY-RULES' Capability Rule, applied to a one-line transform (B9-AC-21).
_capture.key_order: expected_body is a STRING, not an object, because key order is part of the claim: {subject, topic, message} in that order at :106. Dart Map literals preserve insertion order and jsonEncode respects it, so asserting the encoded string gates the order for free (B9-AC-23, F0 § 6.2.3).
